name: TLV70033DCKR
title: TLV700: 200 mA low-IQ low-dropout regulator, fixed outputs 1.2 V to 4.8 V
summary: The TLV700 family are fixed-output PMOS linear regulators for up to 200 mA, running from 2 V to 5.5 V and drawing 31 µA typical with no load. Output voltage is set at the factory between 1.2 V and 4.8 V (the TLV70033 gives 3.3 V) and held within ±2 % over -40 °C to 125 °C junction. They are stable with as little as 0.1 µF of effective output capacitance, have an active-high enable that cuts supply current to about 1 µA, and protect themselves with current limit, thermal shutdown and undervoltage lockout. Packages are a 5-pin SC70 (DCK), a 5-pin SOT-23 (DDC) and a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm 6-pin WSON (DSE).

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The regulator alone with its two capacitors: the supply comes in on IN with CIN to ground, the regulated rail leaves OUT with a 1 µF ceramic COUT to ground, and EN is driven by an on/off control signal. The worked example targets 1.8 V out at 100 mA from a 2.5 V to 3.3 V supply.

parts.note: ceramic; 0.1 µF to 1 µF low-ESR is the range given for the input

notes: The SC70 and SOT-23 parts have one NC pin and the WSON two; an NC pin may be tied to ground for heat dissipation.

equations.name: Output in current limit
equations.note: The output is no longer regulated while the part is limiting current.

operation.text: Inside are a bandgap reference, an error amplifier driving a PMOS pass transistor between IN and OUT, a resistor divider from OUT to ground, and current-limit, thermal-shutdown, undervoltage-lockout and logic blocks; EN connects to the bandgap. Accuracy is 2 % overall, and the output holds its specified accuracy with no load.

In an overload the output delivers a roughly constant current, close to independent of output voltage, and the output voltage falls to whatever that current makes across the load. The pass transistor then dissipates (VIN - VOUT) × ICL; if that heats the die to the shutdown point the part turns off, cools, turns back on, and keeps cycling between limit and shutdown for as long as the fault lasts.

The PMOS pass device has a body diode from OUT to IN. If OUT is held above IN, current flows back through it with no limit. Where reverse voltage can last, the reverse current should be held to 5 % of rated output current by external means.

EN is active high: above 0.9 V the part runs, below 0.4 V it is off and the ground current drops to about 1 µA (400 nA typical at VIN = 2 V). EN may be wired to IN when no shutdown is needed. The EN rating is the lower of VIN + 0.3 V and 6 V.
The output is held off until the input is high enough for the internal circuits to work; the lockout releases at 1.9 V typical with VIN rising.

When VIN - VOUT falls below the dropout voltage, the pass transistor is fully on and behaves as its on-resistance, so dropout grows about in proportion to load current. The output then follows the input less the dropout, and PSRR and transient response get worse as the headroom shrinks toward dropout; line and load steps in dropout can move the output a long way.
The part holds its nominal output when the input exceeds the nominal output plus dropout, the load is under the current limit, and the input is above the lockout level.

1 µF X5R or X7R ceramic capacitors are the recommended choice, since their value and ESR change little with temperature. The loop is stable with any dielectric provided the effective capacitance, after DC-bias and temperature derating, stays at 0.1 µF or more; a part rated 0.1 µF is not enough on its own. ESR must be below 200 mΩ.

No input capacitor is needed for stability in general, but 0.1 µF to 1 µF of low-ESR capacitance from IN to GND improves transient response, noise and ripple rejection and tames reactive sources. A larger value helps with fast, large load steps or when the regulator is far from its source. With a source impedance above 2 Ω, 0.1 µF at the input may be required for stability.
A larger output capacitor lowers the overshoot and undershoot after a load step but makes the recovery last longer.
IN should be fed directly from a supply with low output impedance; inductance between source and IN can cause large voltage swings at IN during start-up and load steps.

Both capacitors go as close to their pins as possible. For best PSRR, noise and transient response, the input and output sides get separate ground planes that meet only at the GND pin, and the output capacitor's ground returns straight to GND. High-ESR capacitors can reduce PSRR.

The output is switched off when the junction reaches about 160 °C and back on at about 140 °C, so an overheated part cycles. The junction should be kept at 125 °C or below; with the worst-case load, shutdown should not occur until at least 35 °C above the highest expected ambient. Running into thermal shutdown repeatedly shortens the part's life, and the protection is not a substitute for heatsinking.

Dissipation is the output current times the drop across the pass element. Heat leaves through the copper around the part, so clear board area, heavier copper and plated vias into inner heat-spreading layers all lower the junction temperature. The thermal table gives the figures for each package on a JEDEC board.
Evaluation boards are offered as TLV70033EVM-503, TLV70018EVM-503 and TLV70028EVM-463 (user guides SLUU391 and SLUU390), and a SPICE model of the TLV700 exists.
